back: P = problems solvable in polynomial time. NP = problems whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time.

front: What does it mean for a problem to be NP-complete?
back: It is in NP (verifiable in poly time) AND NP-hard (every problem in NP reduces to it in poly time) — the hardest problems in NP.

front: If a single NP-complete problem were solved in polynomial time, what would follow?
back: P = NP, and every problem in NP would also be solvable in polynomial time.

front: What is the seed NP-complete problem most reductions chain back to?
back: SAT (Boolean satisfiability), proven NP-complete directly via the Cook-Levin theorem.

front: Practically, what should you reach for when a problem is shown NP-complete?
back: Approximation algorithms, heuristics/metaheuristics, or exact exponential-time algorithms with pruning (backtracking) for small inputs.

front: Name at least three classic NP-complete problems.
back: SAT, 3SAT, 3-Coloring, Hamiltonian Cycle, TSP, Vertex Cover, Independent Set, Knapsack (decision version).

front: If a known NP-complete problem A reduces to a new problem X, what can you immediately conclude about X?
back: X is NP-hard — you never need to re-derive hardness from scratch once a single reduction chain connects back to a known NP-complete problem.

front: What does a decision problem's output always look like, and how does every computation problem relate to it?
back: A 0/1 (yes/no) answer. Every computation problem can be reformulated as an equivalent decision problem.

front: If L1 ≤P L2, what can you conclude about their complements L1-bar and L2-bar?
back: L1-bar ≤P L2-bar also holds — the same reduction function f works, since x ∈ L1 ⟺ f(x) ∈ L2 negates directly to x ∉ L1 ⟺ f(x) ∉ L2.

front: Prove: if a specific NP-complete problem L is in P, what follows?
back: P = NP. Any L' in NP reduces to L (NP-completeness), and L has a poly-time solver (L in P) — chaining the reduction with the solver gives a poly-time solver for L', so all of NP is in P.

front: Is the polynomial-time reduction relation ≤P transitive?
back: Yes — if L1 ≤P L2 via f1 and L2 ≤P L3 via f2, then L1 ≤P L3 via f3 = f2∘f1 (composing two poly-time functions is still poly-time).

front: Shortest simple path vs. longest simple path — complexity class of each, and why the gap?
back: Shortest: in P (Dijkstra/Bellman-Ford). Longest: NP-complete. Shortest-path has optimal substructure; longest-path must avoid revisiting nodes, forcing reasoning over exponentially many node subsets.

front: 2-SAT vs. 3-SAT — complexity class of each, and why the gap?
back: 2-SAT: in P (via implication graphs + SCCs). 3-SAT: NP-complete (the canonical NP-complete problem, alongside SAT). 2-literal clauses only encode pairwise implications, checkable via graph connectivity; 3-literal clauses interlink variables in a way no such shortcut handles.

front: 2-colorability vs. 3-colorability of a graph — complexity class of each, and why the gap?
back: 2-colorability (bipartiteness): in P via BFS/DFS, O(V+E). 3-colorability: NP-complete (one of Karp's original 21). With 2 colors, a vertex's color forces its neighbors' colors deterministically; with 3, neighbors keep 2 open options, creating a genuine exponential branching search.

front: To prove HAM-PATH (Hamiltonian path exists) is in NP, what certificate do you use and what does the verifier check?
back: Certificate: a candidate vertex sequence p. Verifier checks (all poly-time): p has the right number of vertices, all vertices are in G, consecutive pairs are edges, and all vertices in p are distinct — together these ARE the definition of a Hamiltonian path.

front: Is the Hamiltonian Path problem solvable in polynomial time on a DAG?
back: Yes — topologically sort (O(V+E)), then check if every consecutive pair in that order is an edge. A Hamiltonian path in a DAG must follow the topological order, so it's the only candidate to check.
